related.why: The limping child: another paediatric presentation where the history must match the injury
Consent and parental responsibility in a child

brief.role: Core surgical trainee in trauma and orthopaedics
brief.scenario: Leo Denholm, 6 months, has a swollen left thigh. He is not yet crawling or pulling to stand. X-ray shows a spiral fracture of the left femoral shaft. His mother first said she found him crying in his cot this morning; she later said he may have rolled off the sofa yesterday. He has had IV analgesia and a splint. The paediatric registrar is on the way.
brief.task: Speak to Leo's mother, Ms Denholm, about the X-ray and what happens next. The examiner may ask you questions at the end.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: An unexplained fracture in a baby who isn't mobile is a safeguarding concern. Be honest and open with her: don't accuse, and don't hide it.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Telling her the tests are 'routine', or saying 'someone has hurt him'.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Sit down, introduce yourself, ask how Leo is and what she has been told.

grid.label: Opening and the fracture
grid.fail: Starts with the safeguarding process, or explains the X-ray in jargon.
grid.pass: Introduces self, checks what she knows, explains plainly that Leo's thigh bone is broken and his pain is controlled.
grid.high: Asks if she wants anyone with her, and puts Leo's comfort first: pain relief, splint, and a plan for the fracture.

grid.label: Explaining the concern honestly
grid.fail: Accuses ('someone did this'), or hides the concern by calling the tests routine.
grid.pass: Says honestly that this break is not explained by what happened, in a baby not yet mobile, so doctors must look carefully.
grid.high: Explains the same process applies to any baby with an unexplained fracture; is open that children's social care will be involved.

grid.label: Differential diagnosis
grid.fail: Considers only abuse, or only an accident.
grid.pass: Inflicted injury; accidental injury matching the history; bone fragility such as osteogenesis imperfecta or metabolic bone disease.
grid.high: Suspect maltreatment when there is no fragile-bone condition or the explanation is absent or unsuitable; a changing account is unsuitable.

grid.label: Investigations
grid.fail: Plans no further tests, or offers to look at his eyes himself.
grid.pass: Led by the consultant paediatrician: skeletal survey, CT head (under 1 year), ophthalmology examination, bone blood tests.
grid.high: Follow-up skeletal survey at 11–14 days; ophthalmology within 24 hours; written parental consent for the imaging.

grid.label: Escalation and referral
grid.fail: Lets him home, or waits for test results before telling anyone.
grid.pass: Admits under paediatrics; tells the consultant and safeguarding team; referral to children's social care, within 24 hours.
grid.high: Asks about other children at home; does not delay referral for results; would share without consent if asking increased risk.

grid.label: Her distress
grid.fail: Argues with her, or promises social care won't be involved.
grid.pass: Acknowledges her feelings, stays calm, repeats the reason without blame, makes no promises he can't keep.
grid.high: Names her fear that Leo will be taken away; explains social workers assess and support; gives a named contact.

grid.label: Documentation
grid.fail: Writes 'NAI' as a conclusion, or records nothing.
grid.pass: Contemporaneous, dated, timed and signed notes of the history, who gave it, and the findings.
grid.high: Records her exact words in quotation marks, and when and how the account changed.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the bone doctors. May I sit down? Would you like anyone with you? Leo's comfortable now with pain relief and a splint. What have you been told? The X-ray shows his thigh bone is broken.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll be honest with you. Babies who aren't crawling yet rarely break this bone, and we don't know how it happened. Whenever that happens, the hospital follows the same process: specialists check him carefully, and a social worker is involved.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Ms Denholm: "Are you going to take him off me?"

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I can see you're frightened that he'll be taken away. The social worker's job is to understand what happened and support you both. I'm not making that decision today. This is the nurse in charge's number.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Inflicted injury is the main concern: no fragile-bone condition is known and the account changed, so it's unsuitable. Also accidental injury, and osteogenesis imperfecta or metabolic bone disease. Tests: skeletal survey with a follow-up at 11 to 14 days, CT head, ophthalmology within 24 hours, bone bloods, with written parental consent.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Are there other children at home? That goes in the referral, which I won't delay for results. I'd share without consent if asking put him at risk. Her exact words, and when the account changed, go in the notes.

failures.move: Telling her 'this is non-accidental injury until proven otherwise'.
failures.consequence: An accusation, not an assessment: it ends her trust and her account before specialists have assessed Leo.

failures.move: Allowing him home, or holding the referral until results return.
failures.consequence: A non-mobile baby with an unexplained fracture goes back to where it happened, unprotected.

failures.move: Doing fundoscopy himself instead of arranging an ophthalmology examination.
failures.consequence: Retinal haemorrhages are missed or recorded unreliably; the finding may be needed as evidence.

failures.move: Promising that social care won't be involved to calm her down.
failures.consequence: A promise he can't keep; trust breaks down when the referral happens.

recovery.line: Let me put that better: I'm not blaming anyone. We don't know how this happened, and we have to find out.
I can't promise what others will decide, but I will tell you honestly what happens next.

knowledge.fact: Suspect maltreatment if a child has a fracture with no fragile-bone condition, or the explanation is absent or unsuitable (implausible, inadequate or inconsistent).
Under 1 year with suspected physical abuse: skeletal survey and CT head; follow-up imaging ideally 11–14 days later, even if the first survey is normal.
Under 2 years: ophthalmology examination within 24 hours; bone bloods taken at the time of the skeletal survey.
Refer to children's social care immediately if significant harm is suspected; consent is not needed to share information for safeguarding if there is a lawful basis.
Seek consent to share unless asking or delay would increase the risk of harm; explain afterwards unless that increases risk.

recall.think: Unexplained fracture in a non-mobile baby: risk of further serious harm.
recall.say: "We don't know how this happened, so specialists must check him. I'm not blaming anyone."
do: Skeletal survey, CT head, eyes, bone bloods
Social care referral; her exact words in notes
recall.trap: A plausible-sounding story that doesn't fit his development.
recall.finish: Paediatric-led assessment, social care referral, honest communication.

partner.opening: Ms Denholm is waiting in the relatives' room. Leo is asleep in the cubicle next door. Please begin when you're ready.
partner.actorBrief: You are Kayleigh Denholm, 24, Leo's mother. You are tired and anxious. Opening line: "Is he going to be OK? Can I take him home?" If the candidate explains the break plainly, you listen. If more tests or a social worker are mentioned, you become defensive: "Are you saying I hurt my baby?" If the candidate accuses you, cry and stop engaging. If the candidate is calm and honest, you settle a little. Hidden facts, given only if asked: your partner Jordan looked after Leo alone yesterday evening; you have a 3-year-old daughter at nursery whom you must collect at 3 pm. Hidden fear, revealed only if the candidate asks what worries you: that Leo will be taken away. At the end, the examiner asks questions.

reveals.trigger: Asks what she has been told
reveals.finding: "Just that he's got a break and a doctor is coming."
"I found him crying in his cot. Maybe he rolled off the sofa yesterday? Jordan had him last night."

push.question: What is your differential diagnosis?
push.expect: Inflicted injury, accident matching the history, fragile bones (osteogenesis imperfecta, metabolic bone disease).

push.question: What investigations will he need?
push.expect: Paediatric-led: skeletal survey and repeat at 11–14 days, CT head, ophthalmology within 24 hours, bone bloods.

push.question: Who needs to know, and by when?
push.expect: Both consultants, safeguarding team, children's social care referral within 24 hours; ask about siblings.

push.question: What will you document?
push.expect: Contemporaneous, signed notes; her exact words; when the account changed.

curveballs.safeAnswer: Explains calmly he needs to stay for pain control and tests; escalates at once to the consultant and social care. Staff don't restrain; police can take powers of protection if needed.

curveballs.prompt: "Can't you just write that it was an accident?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: he records what he was told and found, honestly, and explains why.

curveballs.prompt: Examiner: Would you check his fundi yourself?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: a dilated examination by an ophthalmologist, within 24 hours.

curveballs.prompt: "He rolled off the sofa. That's what did it."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Doesn't argue or agree; says the specialists will look at everything, which is why the tests matter.
